claims.claim: ANSI/NISO Z39.18 makes a summary a required component of a scientific or technical report, and defines its content as the problem under investigation, the principal results and conclusions, and a recommended course of action for decision makers.

Under the same standard the summary must be independent from the reader's point of view - all symbols, abbreviations and acronyms defined, no cross-references - and a separate executive summary aimed at a management audience is commonly prepared when a print report exceeds 50 pages.

Z39.18 requires a Methods, Assumptions, and Procedures section that identifies the system of measurement used, prefers SI units, requires units to be indicated in a table's title, column heads or a note, and directs that displayed equations be numbered and their symbols defined when a report carries extensive notation.
Z39.18 distinguishes the jobs of figures and tables: graphs show relationships among data, while a table is the better choice when the reader needs highly accurate readings.

The NASA Systems Engineering Handbook fixes the modal-verb convention for requirements - shall states a requirement, will states a fact or declaration of purpose, should states a goal - and directs that requirements be written in the active voice in the form 'responsible party shall perform such and such', one thought per statement, free of ambiguous terms such as 'as appropriate', 'etc.' and 'and/or'.

The same handbook's requirements-validation checklist asks explicitly whether all assumptions have been stated, and treats design reviews as events with a defined purpose, entry and success criteria whose outputs include reports capturing results, recommendations, actions, decision rationale and assumptions.

The Rogers Commission found that on the night of 27 January 1986 managers compared, as a function of temperature, only the flights on which O-ring thermal distress had been observed, rather than the frequency of occurrence across all flights.

Considering the full flight history, the Commission reported three incidents of O-ring thermal distress in twenty flights at joint temperatures of 66 F (18.9 C) or above, against thermal distress on all four flights at 63 F (17.2 C) or below, and concluded that a careful analysis of the flight history would have revealed the correlation of O-ring damage and low temperature, which neither NASA nor Thiokol had carried out.

A later peer-reviewed statistical analysis of the 23 pre-accident launches found strong statistical evidence of a temperature effect on O-ring thermal distress and estimated at least a 0.13 probability of catastrophic field-joint O-ring failure at the 31 F (-0.6 C) launch condition, against at least 0.02 at 60 F (15.6 C).

The reading of Challenger as primarily a failure of graphical presentation is contested: Robison, Boisjoly, Hoeker and Young argue the Thiokol engineers recommended against launch because the projected temperature lay far outside their field database and because they had requested, but not received, data needed to explain the previous January's blow-by.

The Columbia Accident Investigation Board reproduced a Debris Assessment Team briefing slide titled 'Review Of Test Data Indicates Conservatism for Tile Penetration' whose own text gave the ramp volume as 1920 cubic inches against 3 cubic inches for the test data, and concluded that the endemic use of PowerPoint briefing slides in place of technical papers illustrated problematic methods of technical communication at NASA.

The Crater model's test projectiles reached a maximum volume of 3 cubic inches (49 cm3), so the 1920 cubic inch (0.031 m3) figure on the slide represents a 640-fold extrapolation, and the Board recorded that outside its validated limits Crater's precision is unknown.

Crowd-sourced experiments found that truncating a chart's y-axis raises the subjective effect size readers perceive, and that the effect persists even when the design carries explicit visual cues that truncation has occurred; the authors also note truncation is not always deceptive and depends on communicative intent.

The NSPE Code of Ethics requires engineers to be objective and truthful in professional reports, statements or testimony, to include all relevant and pertinent information, to date such reports, and to express technical opinions publicly only when founded upon knowledge of the facts and competence in the subject matter.

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 34(a)(1)(A) allows a party to demand production of documents and electronically stored information including writings, drawings, graphs, charts, photographs, sound recordings, images and other data compilations stored in any medium, which is why ordinary engineering email, tickets and notebooks can become evidence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much of the Challenger launch decision is explained by how the O-ring data were presented
positions: The Rogers Commission recorded that only the flights showing thermal distress were compared against temperature, and concluded a careful analysis of the whole flight history would have revealed the correlation with low temperature - a finding about the analysis and its presentation.
Dalal, Fowlkes and Hoadley demonstrated that the full 23-flight record carried strong statistical evidence of a temperature effect, implying the information needed was available and recoverable.

Robison, Boisjoly, Hoeker and Young argue the engineers did what they were professionally obliged to do: they recommended against launch on the grounds that the projected temperature was far outside their database, and they lacked data they had formally requested. On this reading the decisive failure was in the review and management process, not in the engineers' charts.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states what the Commission and the later statistical work establish - that the incident-only comparison hid a pattern the full record contains - and explicitly says that scholarship disputes the stronger claim that better charts alone would have changed the outcome. The professional-conduct dimension is handed to engineering-ethics.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether truncating a chart axis is always dishonest
positions: Truncation reliably inflates perceived effect size, and warning cues do not neutralize it.
The same authors present cases where truncation is beneficial, and argue the scale should match the size of the effect and variation the author intends to communicate.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the rule as 'label the axis, show the baseline, and choose the scale around the effect that matters' rather than 'always start at zero', which matches what the evidence actually supports.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing checkable about engineering communication; its body was subject-agnostic boilerplate ('a concept students use to organize information') that no source supports and that could describe any topic.
The draft's toolbox-drawer analogy and map-legend analogy did not describe engineering documents at all and were discarded.
The draft had no analogyLimits, no worked example, only four vocabulary terms and three-option questions - none of which met the schema.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with sourced material built on ANSI/NISO Z39.18, the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, the Rogers Commission report and the CAIB report.
Grounded the Challenger case in the Commission's own Chapter VI numbers (3 of 20 flights at 66 F and above; 4 of 4 at 63 F and below) rather than in a general claim that 'the charts were bad'.
Added the contested-scholarship caveat so the lesson does not adopt any single account of the charts.
Converted the worked example into real before-and-after document text using the Columbia briefing slide reproduced in CAIB Volume I, with the rewrite clearly labelled as this lesson's reconstruction.
Handed significant figures and uncertainty arithmetic to the merged units topic instead of re-teaching them.
rightsIssues: ANSI/NISO Z39.18 is copyrighted; its own notice permits accurate noncommercial reproduction with attribution, but nothing beyond short attributed phrases is reproduced here and the usage is recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY.
The NSPE Code of Ethics is copyrighted; only two short attributed phrases from Rules of Practice 3(a) and 3(b) appear.

The Dalal (1989) and Robison (2002) papers are paywalled journal articles used as REFERENCE_ONLY; the Dalal full text was read from an open university course copy and the Robison abstract from the PubMed record, with the DOIs registered as canonical.

The Debris Assessment Team slide quoted in the worked example is reproduced inside CAIB Volume I, a U.S. Government work; the quotation is limited to the slide's title line and one numeric bullet, both attributed.

sourceRecords.title: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, Volume I (June 6, 1986)
sourceRecords.provider: Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident (NASA History Office electronic edition)
sourceRecords.license: Work of the United States Government; no copyright asserted on the electronic edition
sourceRecords.notes: Chapter V (v1ch5.htm) and Chapter VI (v1ch6.htm) fetched with curl and converted to text. Chapter V opens 'The decision to launch the Challenger was flawed' (p. 82) and records the two-phase January 27, 1986 teleconference, the Thiokol charts arriving at Kennedy by telefax, Boisjoly's testimony that when asked to quantify his concern he could not, and the initial engineering recommendation not to fly below 53 degrees Fahrenheit. Chapter VI ('Temperature Effects', pp. 143-148) supplies the data-presentation finding: managers 'compared as a function of temperature the flights for which thermal distress of O-rings had been observed-not the frequency of occurrence based on all flights (Figure 6)'; with all flights included (Figure 7) 'only three incidents of O-ring thermal distress occurred out of twenty flights with O-ring temperatures at 66 degrees Fahrenheit or above, whereas, all four flights with O-ring temperatures at 63 degrees Fahrenheit or below experienced O-ring thermal distress', and conclusion 6 states 'A careful analysis of the flight history of O-ring performance would have revealed the correlation of O-ring damage and low temperature. Neither NASA nor Thiokol carried out such an analysis'. Facts synthesized; only short attributed phrases quoted.

sourceRecords.title: Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Volume I (August 2003)
sourceRecords.license: Work of the United States Government; no copyright asserted
sourceRecords.notes: 248-page PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally. Chapter 6 records that Crater's test projectiles had a maximum volume of 3 cubic inches and that 'When used outside its validated limits, Crater's precision is unknown.' Chapter 7 (p. 191, the 'Engineering by Viewgraph' box) reproduces the Debris Assessment Team slide titled 'Review Of Test Data Indicates Conservatism for Tile Penetration', which states 'Volume of ramp is 1920cu in vs 3 cu in for test', and carries the Board's own finding: 'The Board views the endemic use of PowerPoint briefing slides instead of technical papers as an illustration of the problematic methods of technical communication at NASA', preceded by 'As information gets passed up an organization hierarchy... key explanations and supporting information is filtered out.' Chapter 7 also notes the Naval Reactors practice of documenting technical recommendations in peer-reviewed formal written correspondence rather than briefings. Only short attributed phrases quoted.

sourceRecords.title: ANSI/NISO Z39.18-2005 (R2010), Scientific and Technical Reports - Preparation, Presentation, and Preservation
sourceRecords.provider: National Information Standards Organization (NISO) / American National Standards Institute
sourceRecords.license: Copyright 2010 NISO. The document's own notice permits reproduction for noncommercial purposes only, provided it is reproduced accurately, the source is identified, and NISO copyright status is acknowledged.
sourceRecords.notes: 96-page PDF (groups.niso.org/higherlogic/ws/public/download/12038/Z39_18_2005_R2010.pdf, linked from the NISO landing page registered here) downloaded and text-extracted locally. Supports: the summary as a required report component stating the problem, principal results and conclusions, and a recommended course of action for decision makers (5.2.1); the summary and abstract being independent of the text with all symbols and acronyms defined (5.1.6, 5.2.1); the separate executive summary for a management audience when a report exceeds 50 pages; the required 'Methods, Assumptions, and Procedures' section, which also requires identifying the system of measurement (5.2.3); the introduction naming the report's audience (5.2.2); figure and table guidance including descriptive titles, units given in table titles, column heads or a note, keys for symbols not defined in the text, and using a table rather than a graph when highly accurate readings are needed (6.2); SI as the preferred unit standard (6.5); numbering all displayed equations in a report with extensive notation and defining symbols below the equation (6.6); and a list of symbols, abbreviations, and acronyms when more than five appear (6.9). No standard text reproduced beyond short attributed phrases.

sourceRecords.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, NASA/SP-2016-6105 Rev 2
sourceRecords.license: Work of the United States Government; no copyright asserted
sourceRecords.notes: 297-page PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally. Appendix C, 'How to Write a Good Requirement - Checklist', supplies the modal-verb convention (shall = requirement, will = fact or declaration of purpose, should = goal), the instruction to write requirements in the active rather than the passive voice as 'responsible party shall perform such and such', the demand for one thought per requirement statement with one subject and one predicate, the ban on indefinite pronouns and ambiguous terms such as 'as appropriate', 'etc.', and 'and/or', the requirement that tolerances accompany performance values, and the validation-checklist item 'Have all assumptions been explicitly stated?'. Section 6.7 supports design reviews as scheduled events with a stated purpose, objective, and entry and success criteria, producing technical review reports capturing results, recommendations, actions, decision rationale, and assumptions.

sourceRecords.title: Risk Analysis of the Space Shuttle: Pre-Challenger Prediction of Failure
sourceRecords.provider: Journal of the American Statistical Association 84(408): 945-957 (Dalal, Fowlkes and Hoadley)
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read from an open university course copy (https://www.sfu.ca/~joanh/stat475-675/DalalEtAl_JASA1989.pdf); the DOI record is registered as the canonical location. Supports: using the 23 pre-accident launches, binomial and binary logistic regression show strong statistical evidence of a temperature effect on O-ring thermal distress; a probabilistic risk assessment at 31 F gives at least a 0.13 probability of catastrophic field-joint O-ring failure, and postponement to 60 F would have reduced it to at least 0.02. The paper's Figure 1 contrasts panel (a), the incident-only plot, with panel (b), which 'includes flights with no incidents', and it attributes the omission finding to the Rogers Commission report. Used here only for the data-presentation point and the magnitude of the temperature effect; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Representation and misrepresentation: Tufte and the Morton Thiokol engineers on the Challenger
sourceRecords.provider: Science and Engineering Ethics 8(1): 59-81 (Robison, Boisjoly, Hoeker and Young)
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract and full bibliographic record retrieved from the NCBI E-utilities PubMed record (PMID 11840958); full text is paywalled and was not read. Cited only for the position it takes: the authors, one of whom is Roger Boisjoly himself, argue against reading the Challenger charts as a simple failure of graphical presentation, holding that the engineers recommended against launch because the projected temperature was far outside their field database and that they had asked for, but not received, data needed to explain the previous January's blow-by. Used to prevent the lesson from overstating any single account of the charts.

sourceRecords.title: Truncating the Y-Axis: Threat or Menace?
sourceRecords.provider: Correll, Bertini and Franconeri; arXiv:1907.02035 (later published at ACM CHI 2020)
sourceRecords.license: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license (Nonexclusive-distrib 1.0) as shown on the abstract page
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract page read. Supports the claim that a y-axis not beginning at zero can visually exaggerate effect size, that the authors' crowd-sourced experiments found the subjective impact of axis truncation persistent across visualization designs even when explicit visual cues signal the truncation, and their recommendation that designers choose scales around the size of the effects and variation they intend to communicate. Also supports the honest caveat that truncation is not always deceptive and can be appropriate depending on analytic intent.

sourceRecords.title: Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Rule 34: Producing Documents, Electronically Stored Information, and Tangible Things
sourceRecords.provider: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts
sourceRecords.license: United States federal rule text; not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Rule text read at Cornell Legal Information Institute (https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_34) because the uscourts.gov landing page registered here serves the rules as a PDF set; the canonical publisher URL is recorded in the url field. Rule 34(a)(1)(A) lets a party request 'any designated documents or electronically stored information - including writings, drawings, graphs, charts, photographs, sound recordings, images, and other data or data compilations - stored in any medium'. Used only to support the narrow claim that ordinary engineering working records are the kind of material a civil litigant can compel; the lesson gives no legal advice.

sourceRecords.title: NSPE Code of Ethics for Engineers
sourceRecords.notes: Official NSPE PDF retrieved with a browser user-agent and read. For this topic the load-bearing provisions are Rule of Practice 3(a) - engineers shall be objective and truthful in professional reports, statements or testimony, shall include all relevant and pertinent information, and the report 'should bear the date indicating when it was current' - and Rule of Practice 3(b), that engineers may express technical opinions publicly only when founded upon knowledge of the facts and competence in the subject matter. Professional Obligation 9 requires giving credit for engineering work to those to whom it is due. Copyrighted NSPE publication; only short attributed phrases quoted.
